summary: A scholar in Buddhist and religious studies, John S. Strong studied at Oberlin, Hartford Seminary, and the University of Chicago under J. A. B. van Buitenen and Frank E. Reynolds. He served at Bates College as Dana Professor of Religious Studies (1987-1988).

Working in linguistics and Indology, John Sampson earned degrees from the University of Liverpool and the University of Oxford. He served as the Librarian at the University of Liverpool from 1892 to 1928.

An Indology and linguistics scholar, John Scudder Chandler studied at Yale University. He served as acting principal at Pasumalai Seminary (1890-1892), Fellow at the University of Madras (1913-1922), and director of the Language School at Kodaikanal (1924-1928).

Working in linguistics and Indology, John Shakespear studied at Wellington College, the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst, and under John Richardson. He was Professor of Oriental Languages at Sandhurst (1805-1809) and Professor of Hindustani at Addiscombe Military Seminary (1809-1829).
A scholar in Indology and history/archaeology, John Shore succeeded William Jones and served as President of The Asiatic Society in 1794.

Working in Indology and history/archaeology, John Shortt studied at Madras Medical College and the University of Aberdeen. He served as Assistant Apothecary for the East India Company (~1846-1854) and Assistant Surgeon at the University of Madras (1854-1878).

A scholar of religious studies and Indology, John Sinclair Stevenson studied at Clifton College, Lincoln College, the University of Edinburgh, and Princeton Theological Seminary. He served as a missionary with the Presbyterian Church in Ireland from 1894 to 1924.
Specializing in Buddhist studies, John Snelling served as General Secretary of the Buddhist Society (~1980-1984) and editor of The Middle Way (~1980-1990).

A scholar in Indology and linguistics, John Stevenson studied at the universities of Glasgow and Edinburgh. He served as a missionary for the Scottish Missionary Society (~1823-1834), an East India Company chaplain (1834-1854), and President of the Asiatic Society of Mumbai (~1850-1855).

Working in Indology and religious studies, John Stirling Morley Hooper studied at Corpus Christi College, Oxford. He served as Headmaster of Wesley Higher Secondary School in 1930 and General Secretary of the Bible Society of India in 1941.

A linguist, John Strachan studied at Aberdeen, Cambridge, and Jena under Berthold Delbrück and Rudolf Thurneysen. He was a Fellow at Pembroke College, Cambridge (1886) and held professorships in Greek (1885) and Sanskrit and Comparative Philology (1889) at Owens College.

An Indology and religious studies scholar, John Stratton Hawley studied at Amherst College and under Daniel H. H. Ingalls. He taught at Bowdoin College (~1974-1977) before becoming the Claire Tow Professor of Religion at Columbia University (~1986).
A philosopher and historian who studied at University College London, John Stuart Mill served at the East India Company from circa 1823 to 1858.

A scholar of history and archaeology, John Sydenham Furnivall studied at Trinity Hall, Trinity College, Cambridge, and Leiden University. He founded the Burma Research Society in 1910 and held a post at the University of Cambridge (~1935-1941).

An Indologist and philosopher, John Taber earned his doctorate from the University of Hamburg, studying with Srinivasa Ayya Srinivasan, Lambert Schmithausen, Albrecht Wezler, and Reiner Wiehl. He held posts at Case Western Reserve University (~1983-1989) and the University of New Mexico (~1989).
A scholar of Indology and philosophy, John Taylor earned his M.D. from the University of Edinburgh in 1804 and served with the London Missionary Society from 1805 to 1807.

An Indology scholar, John Thayer Hitchcock studied at Amherst, Chicago, Connecticut, and Cornell. He held academic posts at Amherst, UC Berkeley, and UCLA before serving as Professor of Anthropology and South Asian Studies at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (1966-1982).

Specializing in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, John Thompson Platts studied at Bedford School and Balliol College, Oxford. He held principal and mathematics positions in India before becoming Teacher of Persian at the University of Oxford in 1880.

An Indology and linguistics scholar, John Van Someren Pope studied at the University of Cambridge. He served as a Professor at Presidency University and as Reader in Modern East Indian Languages at Trinity College Dublin (1913).
A scholar of Indology and linguistics, John Victor Boulton completed his Ph.D. at SOAS University of London and served there as Lecturer in Bengali and Oriya from 1962 to 1988.
